pages.x: In 1467 a quarrel over who would be the next shogun split the great lords into two camps and set them fighting in the streets of Kyoto. After ten years the capital lay in ashes and no one had won. The shoguns lost control, and Japan broke up into the lands of rival warlords, the daimyo.

For a century the daimyo fought for land, castles and survival. Vassals overthrew their lords, which the Japanese called gekokujo, the low overthrowing the high. Even Buddhist temples raised armies of warrior monks.
In 1543 Portuguese traders landed on the island of Tanegashima with matchlock guns. Japanese smiths copied them within a year.
pages.fx: Within decades Japan was making guns by the tens of thousands, and battles were won by massed ranks of musketeers.

pages.x: The first great unifier, Oda Nobunaga, beat a far larger army at Okehazama in 1560, took Kyoto in 1568, and in 1575 used volleys of gunfire to crush the famous horsemen of the Takeda at Nagashino. In 1582 one of his own generals turned on him at a temple in Kyoto, and he died in the flames.

Nobunaga's general Hideyoshi, a peasant's son, avenged him and finished uniting Japan by 1590. He took away the peasants' swords and froze everyone in their class, so that no one could rise as he had.

Hideyoshi died in 1598, leaving a five-year-old heir, and the daimyo split again. On 21 October 1600, in fog, at Sekigahara, Tokugawa Ieyasu beat the lords of the west, helped when several of them changed sides in the middle of the battle.

Ieyasu became shogun in 1603. In 1615 he took Osaka castle and wiped out Hideyoshi's family. A Japanese saying sums up the three: Nobunaga pounded the rice, Hideyoshi kneaded the cake, and Ieyasu sat down and ate it.

The Tokugawa shoguns gave Japan more than 250 years of peace, until 1868, and shut it off from most of the world. The age of warring states, with its castles, samurai and ninja, is still the favourite setting of Japanese novels, films and games.
